title: "Copyright and Licensing"
toc: true
---

## Overview

CERTH's Open Science commitments, aligned with the
[European Open Science Cloud (EOSC)](https://eosc.eu/) and Horizon Europe requirements, encourage
making software developed in the course of publicly funded research available as open source wherever
possible. Licence selection should involve a consultation with the CERTH OSPO and consider:

- **Dependent software** which you have used in your project.
- **Community norms** within your ecosystem.
- **Which sharing regime** (permissive, weakly-reciprocal, or strongly-reciprocal) aligns with your
  project's objectives (see [Key concepts: Licensing](../key-concepts/licensing.qmd)).
- **Obligations imposed by your funding body** or consortium agreement.

## Licence compatibility

Use a licence approved by the [Open Source Initiative (OSI)](https://opensource.org/licenses) for
CERTH-copyrighted software. Common choices are overviewed here. 

| Licence | Type | Typical use case |
|---|---|---|
| Apache-2.0 | Permissive | General software; maximum adoption; includes patent grant |
| MIT | Permissive | Small utilities and libraries; minimal requirements |
| GPL-3.0 | Strongly reciprocal | Tools where all derivatives must remain open source |
| LGPL-3.0 | Weakly reciprocal | Libraries intended to be linked from proprietary software |

When combining components, for example by reusing/forking and modifying the code of others
license compatibility must be verified before releasing the result.
This is part of your due diligence (see [Key concepts: Due diligence](../key-concepts/due-diligence.qmd)).
A common compatibility matrix is shown below. Note that reused code **must** maintain the original 
license, for example by being accompanied by the exact original license file.

| You want to use... | Under Apache-2.0 | Under MIT | Under GPL-3.0 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Apache-2.0 code | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| MIT code | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| GPL-3.0 code | Only if your project is also GPL-3.0 | Only if your project is also GPL-3.0 | ✓ |
| LGPL-3.0 library | ✓ (dynamic linking) | ✓ (dynamic linking) | ✓ |

::: {.callout-warning}
**It does not suffice to only mention the desired license in a README file. You need to actually
include the license text.**
:::

## Option 1: Add license in code comments

The two most recognized ways of applying licenses are either as code comments or by including 
license files in the source code directory and appropriately marking your files.
The legal text that should go into those files or comments is different by license but typically
requires manually filling out the copyright holder, which is CERTH, and year, which is 
the year of the code's first public release. 

Comment-based licensing requires less book-keeping for small projects. It can thus serve as 
a starting point until the project grows in size, in which case you can move to the option of adding 
license files, as described next. A Python file licensed under Apache-2.0 may look
like this:


```python
# Copyright 2026 Centre for Research and Technology Hellas (CERTH)
# 
# Licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0 (the "License");
# you may not use this file except in compliance with the License.
# You may obtain a copy of the License at
# 
#     http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0
# 
# Unless required by applicable law or agreed to in writing, software
# distributed under the License is distributed on an "AS IS" BASIS,
# WITHOUT WARRANTIES OR CONDITIONS OF ANY KIND, either express or implied.
# See the License for the specific language governing permissions and
# limitations under the License.

name = "the CERTH OSPO"
print(f"Hello from {name}!")
```

## Option 2: Add license files

In larger projects (e.g., with >30 files), you may want to concentrate your licensing information
in one place. Historically, an ad-hoc description would have been provided to describe which
licenses apply to which files or code segments. However, we recommend the 
[REUSE specification](https://reuse.software/) as a recommended standard that is also endorsed by
the Free Software Foundation Europe (FSFE) and broadly adopted in European open-source projects
like the [Linux kernel](https://github.com/torvalds/linux).

This specification requires first gathering all applicable licenses under a `LICENSES/` directory
in the repository root. Licenses should contain the **full licence text** for each
licence used (e.g., `LICENSES/Apache-2.0.txt`).
Then, in each source code file, a copyright notice briefly establishes the ownership
and creation timeframe. Like above, the notice identifies the copyright holder and the year 
the specific file was created.
Again, only the initial year of creation needs to be included. Successive years or ranges are unnecessary
unless the file has been substantially revised by a different contributor, in which case additional
lines can be added:

**Format:**

```text
SPDX-FileCopyrightText: <year> <copyright holder>
```

**Example:**

```text
SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2024 Centre for Research and Technology Hellas (CERTH)
SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2025 Contributor Name, Affiliation
```

The notice by itself does not yet link to a license. This is done by also including
the license notice using an appropriate [SPDX identifier](https://spdx.org/licenses/). Do note
that the license notice is also not sufficient for meeting all legal licensing requirements;
you should also add the used license in the `LICENSES/` directory.

**Format:**

```text
SPDX-License-Identifier: <SPDX-identifier>
```

**Complete example for an Apache-2.0-licensed Python source file:**

```python
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Centre for Research and Technology Hellas (CERTH)
# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0

name = "the CERTH OSPO"
print(f"Hello from {name}!")
```

This machine-readable format enables automated licence compliance verification by tools such as
`reuse lint` and third-party scanners used by downstream integrators. For example, check that 
all your files have been properly annotated with copyright and license by installing the `reuse`
package in your Python virtual environment. The CERTH OSPO can assist with initial setup and 
interpreting results.

```bash
pip install reuse
reuse lint
```

## Placement in source files

Place SPDX tags or license comments in a comment block at the very top of each source file, 
before any other content like imports or package declarations. For file formats that do not support 
inline comments (e.g., images, binary assets, or certain data formats shipped with the software), 
use a companion `.license` sidecar file with the same base name:

```text
my-asset.svg          ← the asset
my-asset.svg.license  ← contains the SPDX tags
```

If you have such files that cannot carry inline notices and are using the REUSE specification, 
you need to state which they are with a `REUSE.toml` file (or legacy `.reuse/dep5`). This is
placed at the root of your project and maps file globs to their copyright and licence information.
